READING

**The fault-line in PENNYQUAY**

The case for PENNYQUAY is presented attractively: lower outage cost (GBP 8,436 vs GBP 19,152), no non-returnable deposit, and a demonstrated Board willingness to accept undertakings. All of that is accurate. But every one of those advantages becomes irrelevant if the course produces a renewal that the bank treats as a covenant trigger.

The scheme's own facts establish the outcome of the undertaking route beyond reasonable doubt. Cadgarth (2024) and Nant Elwy (2025) are not minor precedents; they are the only two filed examples, and both produced a six-year renewal rather than fifteen. A six-year renewal lodged in time to capture a 2028 start date runs to roughly 2034. The loan runs to 2039. The gap is five years. The bank wrote on 2026-06-22 that a licence term shorter than the loan would put the facility under review. PENNYQUAY therefore does not merely risk triggering that letter; it makes triggering it the near-certain outcome.

A "facility under review" for a two-person operator carrying GBP 480,000 of project debt is not a manageable inconvenience. It creates lender discretion to call or restructure the loan at a point when the scheme has no obvious refinancing route, and it persists for five years. Against that exposure, the GBP 10,716 saving on outage losses and the avoidance of the deposit look trivial.

No argument saves PENNYQUAY on this point. The Board may have accepted undertakings, but the Board's preference for them over certificates is settled: it reduces the renewal to six years. You could try to negotiate with the bank to waive the review, but the bank's letter shows it has already identified the issue, and a waiver request advertises the weakness of your position. You could argue that a future fifteen-year renewal after the July 2027 screen installation will remedy the gap, but the licence will then be running on a six-year instrument, and the bank's review clause operates on the licence term at grant, not on a speculative future renewal.

PENNYQUAY is not a close call dressed up as safe. It is a near-certain route to the one outcome the bank has explicitly named as grounds for intervention.

---

**What LINTHAUGH actually costs**

The costs of LINTHAUGH need separating into committed spend and conditional spend.

The GBP 9,000 derogation application is spent on 2026-10-19 regardless of outcome.

The GBP 46,000 deposit is paid on 2026-12-01. If the derogation is granted, this deposit secures the February slot and is part of the installation cost — money spent on the screen, not money lost. If the derogation is refused, it is forfeited, and that GBP 46,000 is a dead loss.

The GBP 19,152 February outage arises only if the derogation is granted and the slot is used. The marginal outage cost over the July alternative is GBP 10,716.

So the LINTHAUGH cost structure, compared with PENNYQUAY, is:

- **If granted:** GBP 9,000 (application) + GBP 10,716 (incremental outage) = GBP 19,716 extra, in exchange for a certificate, a fifteen-year renewal, and no bank review.
- **If refused:** GBP 9,000 + GBP 46,000 (deposit forfeited) = GBP 55,000 extra, and you then proceed via undertaking — same outcome as PENNYQUAY but GBP 55,000 poorer, and you only just make the 2027-05-31 deadline (18 weeks from 2027-01-25 falls exactly on that date).

The downside scenario is therefore painful but survivable: you lose GBP 55,000, you file the undertaking, and you face the bank review that you were always going to face under PENNYQUAY. The scheme continues. You are poorer; you are not destroyed.

---

**Assessing the derogation probability**

The raw grant rate is 4 of 11 (36%). But the Board's own published refusals supply the critical information: every refusal named a scheme with no dated regulatory driver. The Board has effectively published its selection criterion. Blaenclydach has a dated regulatory driver that is impossible to argue away: the abstraction licence renewal must be lodged by 2027-05-31, that filing requires a compliance certificate, and the certificate requires the new screen. The causal chain is locked to a statutory date. This is precisely the characteristic that distinguished granted applications from refused ones.

It would be wrong to claim certainty; the Board granted only 4 of 11 and we do not know whether all 4 had dated drivers or whether some were granted on other grounds. But the logical implication of the published refusal reasoning is that a scheme presenting a clear, documented, dated statutory driver has materially better odds than 36%. A conservative working assumption of 60–70% is supportable; if all four grants went to schemes with dated drivers and all seven refusals went to schemes without, the success rate for applications like Blaenclydach's would be 100% of its comparator group, with the overall 36% rate being an artefact of the mix of applicants rather than a guide to any individual application.

For the deposit decision on 2026-12-01, the relevant question is: does the expected benefit of a successful derogation justify paying GBP 46,000 at risk? The benefit is removing a five-year licence shortfall that triggers a bank review on a GBP 480,000 loan. That exposure, even partially priced, comfortably exceeds GBP 46,000. At 60% grant probability, the expected cost of the deposit-at-risk element is GBP 18,400. The benefit side of the ledger is the avoided bank review, which in a worst case could cost the scheme everything.

---

**The July-slot fallback under LINTHAUGH**

One further point in LINTHAUGH's favour: if the derogation is refused on 2027-01-25, you still have the option of the July 2027 slot (Vossbeck confirms it by 2027-04-30), so you can install the screen in the permitted window after lodging the renewal by undertaking. The fallback is functional, just expensive. Under PENNYQUAY you have no option to achieve a certificate before the renewal deadline at all.

---

**Summary of the decision**

|  | PENNYQUAY | LINTHAUGH (granted) | LINTHAUGH (refused) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Direct extra cost vs doing nothing | GBP 8,436 | GBP 19,716 + deposit absorbed | GBP 55,000 + GBP 8,436 |
| Renewal term | Six years (~2034) | Fifteen years (~2043) | Six years (~2034) |
| Bank review triggered | Almost certain | No | Almost certain |
| Scenario probability | — | ~60–70%+ | ~30–40% |

PENNYQUAY saves GBP 11,280 in direct costs against a successful LINTHAUGH and avoids the deposit risk, but it delivers the bank-review outcome with near certainty. LINTHAUGH pays a modest incremental cost on the likely outcome and limits the downside of the unlikely outcome to one that, while expensive, still leaves the scheme operating.

READING
  PENNYQUAY's apparent cheapness is negated by the established six-year renewal precedent, which triggers the bank's explicitly stated review concern on a loan running five years beyond the likely licence term. LINTHAUGH's derogation application is strong because Blaenclydach possesses the dated regulatory driver that the Board's published refusals show was absent from every rejected scheme, making the expected cost of the deposit-at-risk small against the benefit of a fifteen-year renewal that keeps the bank satisfied. The downside of a refusal — GBP 55,000 lost plus a return to the undertaking route — is painful but does not threaten the scheme's existence, whereas a bank facility review does.

CALL
  LINTHAUGH

GROUNDS
  The undertaking route produces a six-year renewal expiring around 2034, five years short of the 2039 loan, which the bank has already identified as grounds for a facility review; LINTHAUGH, whose derogation application is strongly placed because Blaenclydach has the dated regulatory driver that the Board's own published refusals name as the decisive criterion, is the only course that removes that threat.
